decisionSource: The current codified text of Ohio Rev. Code section 2953.321 and the complete section list of Revised Code chapter 2953, both from the Ohio Legislative Service Commission's own publication at codes.ohio.gov; the complete section list of chapter 3796, the successor to the chapter the 2023 initiated statute enacted; an official archived capture of chapter 3780 as it stood immediately before repeal, listing all 36 of its sections; and the Legislative Service Commission's Final Analysis of Senate Bill 56 of the 136th General Assembly. Read against the integrated Ohio legal-design memo, the normalized track registry, the authoritative blocker ledger and the integrated Ohio automatic-sealing decision.
whatThisDocumentIs: The decision record that answers one release-blocking question on oh_marijuana_expungement: whether Ohio Issue 2 created a separate or automatic record-clearing mechanism alongside the participant application route the memo represents under Ohio Rev. Code section 2953.321. The memo recorded the question in terms that named a secondary policy-centre analysis covering Senate Bill 56 and Issue 2 together, and recorded that the analysis had not been read in full. This record does not resolve it from that analysis. It resolves it from the enacted law: the complete contents of the initiated statute's own chapter, the complete sealing and expungement inventory of chapter 2953, and the Legislative Service Commission's Final Analysis of the act that created the marijuana expungement section. It amends no memo, regenerates no registry, implements nothing and asserts no counsel approval.

scopeOfThisJob.trackTouched: None. This record adjudicates a question about oh_marijuana_expungement and writes only itself.
scopeOfThisJob.questionsExpresslyNotReached: The track's other release blocker — whether Ohio courts have published a dedicated local application form for a section that took effect on 2026-03-20 — is a different question with a different answer and is not resolved here. questionPresented.theQuestion: Whether Ohio Issue 2 created any separate or automatic relief alongside the Ohio Rev. Code section 2953.321 application route.
questionPresented.whyItMattered: If Issue 2 had created an automatic route, the product would be selling an application to people whose records were already clearing, and the track's whole participant-facing posture would be wrong. It is the same failure mode the integrated Ohio automatic-sealing decision was written to prevent, arriving on a different statute.
questionPresented.whyItWasOpen: The memo recorded the question against a secondary source — a policy-centre analysis that discusses Senate Bill 56 and Issue 2 together — and recorded honestly that it had not been read in full. Two things being discussed in one document is not evidence that they are one legal mechanism, and the memo did not treat it as such.

methodNote: The assignment forbids inferring a second route merely because an analysis discusses Issue 2 and Senate Bill 56 together, and forbids treating advocacy commentary as controlling. So the secondary analysis was not read and is not relied on in either direction. The question is answered by enumeration instead, which is the only way to prove this kind of negative: the complete section list of the chapter the initiated statute enacted, captured while it still existed; the complete section list of the chapter that replaced it; and the complete sealing and expungement inventory of chapter 2953. A mechanism that exists has a section. Three complete lists with no such section, plus a Final Analysis that introduces the expungement provision as new, is an affirmative finding rather than a failure to find.
retrievalNote: www.legislature.ohio.gov presents an incomplete TLS chain and both WebFetch and default curl refused it. The Final Analysis was retrieved with certificate verification disabled, which is recorded rather than hidden. Its authenticity is not taken on trust from the transport: the document self-identifies as the Legislative Service Commission's Final Analysis of S.B. 56 of the 136th General Assembly, and every operative fact taken from it — the March 20, 2026 effective date, the $50 fee and its 30/20 split, the 45-to-90-day hearing window, the prosecutor's objection right, and the weighing standard — was independently confirmed against the codified text at codes.ohio.gov, which was retrieved over a valid connection. Nothing rests on the Final Analysis alone except the legislative-history characterisation, which the codified section's own single-version history corroborates.

controllingSources.citation: Ohio Rev. Code § 2953.321, Expungement of marijuana or hashish possession offenses
controllingSources.availableVersions: Exactly one: "March 20, 2026 – Enacted by Senate Bill 56 - 136th General Assembly". There is no earlier version of this section, which is itself evidence that no marijuana expungement provision preceded it.
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Division (B): a person who, prior to the effective date, was the defendant named in a dismissed complaint, indictment or information for, or was convicted of or pleaded guilty to, a violation of division (C)(3)(a) or (C)(7)(a) or (b) of section 2925.11, or a violation of division (C)(7)(c) or (d) of that section involving possession of not more than fifteen grams of hashish, "may file an application under this section requesting an expungement". Division (C): the person "may apply to the sentencing court", may file "at any time on or after the effective date of this section", and the application must identify the applicant and the offence, include evidence that the offence and the disposition fall within the section, and include a request for expungement. Division (D): on filing and payment of the fee the court sets a hearing and notifies the prosecutor, who may object by filing an objection before the hearing date, and the court directs a probation officer to make inquiries and written reports; the hearing is held not less than forty-five and not more than ninety days after filing. Division (E)(3): the court weighs the applicant's interests against the legitimate needs of the government. Division (G): unless indigent the applicant pays a fee of fifty dollars, thirty into the state treasury with half of that credited to the attorney general reimbursement fund and twenty into the county general revenue fund.

controllingSources.citation: Ohio Rev. Code chapter 2953, complete section list
controllingSources.operativeFinding: The chapter page rendered in full on this retrieval, 43 sections from 2953.01 to 2953.84. Exactly one concerns marijuana: section 2953.321. The sealing and expungement inventory is sections 2953.31 definitions, 2953.32 conviction sealing or expungement on application, 2953.321 marijuana and hashish expungement on application, 2953.33 non-conviction sealing on application, 2953.34 effect, 2953.35, 2953.36 and 2953.37, 2953.39 prosecutor-initiated, 2953.521 human trafficking, 2953.57 to 2953.60 the separate post-DNA-testing regime, and 2953.61 the multiple-charge rule. A full-text scan of the chapter for automatic language returned three occurrences of "automatic" and none is a record-clearing mechanism: all three are collateral-sanction language inside the certificate of qualification for employment and the certificate of qualification for housing sections. There is no occurrence of "automatically", "without application", "without a petition" or "on its own motion".
controllingSources.retrievalNote: A prior Ohio job recorded that this chapter page paginates and truncated before section 2953.31. It did not truncate on this retrieval, so the enumeration is first-hand and complete rather than reconstructed section by section.

controllingSources.citation: Ohio Rev. Code chapter 3780, the chapter enacted by the 2023 initiated statute, complete section list as it stood immediately before repeal
controllingSources.issuer: Ohio Legislative Service Commission, codes.ohio.gov, via an official archived capture
controllingSources.whyArchived: codes.ohio.gov no longer serves chapter 3780: a live request returns "No Ohio Revised Code section number corresponds to 3780", because Senate Bill 56 repealed the chapter effective 2026-03-20. The archived capture is of the official publisher's own page, taken two weeks before the repeal took effect, and each section it lists carries the publisher's own repeal notation.
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Thirty-six sections, and this is the decisive enumeration. In order: 3780.01 Definitions, 3780.02 Authorization and purpose, 3780.03 Establishment and authority, 3780.04 Allowable forms of adult use cannabis, 3780.05 Electronic database, 3780.06 Information provided by the division, 3780.07 Facilities, 3780.08 Criminal records checks, 3780.09 Location of adult use cannabis operators, 3780.10 Adult use cannabis operations, 3780.11 Application requirements, 3780.12 to 3780.17 licensure, 3780.20 Operations, 3780.21 Advertising, 3780.22 and 3780.24 tax, 3780.25 Local authority, 3780.26 to 3780.28 enforcement, 3780.29 Home grow, 3780.30 Cannabis addiction services, 3780.31 Confidentiality, 3780.32 Venue for court actions, 3780.33 Liabilities and immunities, 3780.34 Financial institutions, 3780.35 Rights of employer, 3780.36 Limitations on conduct, 3780.37 Drug misuse prevention, 3780.90 Severability and 3780.99 Penalties. Not one concerns expungement, sealing or the clearing of a criminal record. The chapter page contains zero occurrences of "expunge", "expungement", "sealing" or "record of conviction", and no reference to chapter 2953 at all. The twenty-three occurrences of "criminal record" are the licensing background-check provisions at 3780.08 and its cross-references; a criminal records check is the opposite of record clearing.

controllingSources.citation: Ohio Rev. Code chapter 3796, Marijuana Control Program, complete section list
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Thirty-nine sections, none concerning expungement, sealing or record clearing. Zero occurrences of "expunge" or "expungement" and zero references to chapter 2953. The only records-adjacent heading is 3796.12, Criminal records check, which is a licensing background check. The chapter's own text repeatedly refers to "Chapter 3780. of the Revised Code, as that chapter existed immediately prior to the effective date of this amendment", and section 3796.34 carries the heading "[Former R.C. 3780.37, amended and renumbered by S.B. 56, 136th General Assembly, effective 3/20/2026]". This is where the initiated statute's substance now lives.

controllingSources.citation: S.B. 56 Final Analysis, 136th General Assembly, Ohio Legislative Service Commission, Office of Research and Drafting and Legislative Budget Office
controllingSources.documentIdentity: 52 pages; primary sponsor Sen. Huffman; "Effective date: March 20, 2026; operating appropriations effective December 19, 2025"; contains item vetoes.
controllingSources.operativeFinding: Under the heading "Expungement of prior marijuana or hashish possession offenses" the analysis states that the act "permits a person who, prior to March 20, 2026, was a defendant named in a dismissed complaint, indictment, or information for or was convicted of or pled guilty to" a minor misdemeanour marijuana possession offence, a misdemeanour hashish possession offence, or a felony hashish possession offence involving not more than fifteen grams of hashish, "to apply to the sentencing court to have the official record or record of their conviction in the case expunged", footnoted to R.C. 2953.321(B). It then records the $50 fee unless indigent with its 30/20 split, the 45-to-90-day hearing window, the requirement that the court notify the prosecutor and the prosecutor's right to object before the hearing, and the weighing of the applicant's interests against legitimate governmental needs.
controllingSources.theStructuralTell: The analysis footnotes its provisions in a consistent form. Where the act re-enacts something the initiated statute had, the footnote pairs the new section with the old one and marks it repealed — for example "R.C. 3796.06; R.C. 3780.04, repealed" and "R.C. 3796.31(B); R.C. 3780.25(G)(2), repealed". Twenty-six distinct former chapter 3780 sections are cited that way across the document. The expungement footnote is "R.C. 2953.321(B)" alone, with no repealed predecessor, and the analysis introduces the provision with "The act permits" rather than as a continuation. A search of the whole document for any pairing of a 3780 citation with expungement, sealing or record-clearing language returns nothing but one false positive created by two adjacent footnotes on unrelated subjects.

controllingSources.operativeFinding: Already established, and independently, that current Ohio law provides neither automatic sealing nor automatic expungement of an adult criminal record; that every adult route is begun by the person's application or by a prosecutor's motion under section 2953.39 and decided at the court's discretion; and that the one automatic provision, section 2151.356, is juvenile. Its evidence included the Supreme Court of Ohio's own enumeration of every adult rights-restoration and record-sealing route, revised June 2026 — an enumeration published two and a half years after the initiated statute took effect, in which no Issue 2 route appears.
controllingSources.whyItCorroborates: That record answered the general question for the whole state. This record answers the specific question for one statute. They are independent readings reaching the same place, and the June 2026 judicial enumeration is the strongest single piece of evidence that Issue 2 left no record-clearing route behind, because it postdates Issue 2 and would have had to list one.

sourcesExpresslyNotRelieduponAsProof: The policy-centre analysis the memo named was deliberately not read and is not relied on in either direction. The assignment forbids treating advocacy commentary as controlling and forbids inferring a second route merely because an analysis discusses Issue 2 and Senate Bill 56 together. The question is answered from enacted law instead.
No commercial compilation, news report or law-firm page was used to establish any text.
The absence of an agency web page describing automatic marijuana relief is not relied on. The negative rests on three complete statutory enumerations.
The four sibling Ohio routes were not used as an analogy. The assignment forbids it and they are differently drafted; section 2953.321 was read on its own terms.

determination.1_doesMoreThanOneLegalMechanismExist: No. Ohio Rev. Code section 2953.321 is the complete and only mechanism for clearing a marijuana or hashish possession record in Ohio. Chapter 2953 contains exactly one marijuana provision; the chapter the initiated statute enacted contained none across all thirty-six of its sections; and the chapter that replaced it contains none across all thirty-nine of its sections.
determination.2_didIssue2CreateASeparateOrAutomaticMec: No, and it never did. The initiated statute's chapter is now repealed, but its complete contents were captured while it still stood and it contained no expungement, sealing or record-clearing provision of any kind. This is not a finding that a mechanism was created and later removed; it is a finding that none was ever created. Senate Bill 56 repealed chapter 3780 and re-enacted its substance in chapter 3796, and in the same act created section 2953.321 as a new provision with no predecessor.
determination.3_isAnyReliefAutomatic: No. Nothing in section 2953.321 operates without an application. Division (C) requires the person to apply, division (D) conditions the court's first step on "the filing of an application", and there is no provision anywhere in chapter 2953 for a marijuana record to clear on the court's own motion, on an agency's motion, or by operation of law. The one automatic sealing provision in Ohio law remains section 2151.356, and it is juvenile.
determination.4_isAParticipantApplicationRequired: Yes, and it is the whole of the mechanism. The route does not begin until the person files.
determination.5_filingActor: The person themselves — the applicant who was the defendant named in the dismissed charge or who was convicted of or pleaded guilty to the qualifying offence. Section 2953.321 names no probation-officer alternative and no prosecutor-initiated alternative. The prosecutor's only role is to object. This distinguishes it from section 2953.39, where the prosecutor moves and the subject files nothing, and that section reaches low-level controlled substance offences rather than this one.
determination.6_filingCourt: The sentencing court, in the statute's own words: the person "may apply to the sentencing court". For a dismissed charge, the court in which the charges were dismissed, which division (C)(1) requires the application to identify. Statewide in application; the venue follows the participant's own case.
determination.7_discretion: Discretionary, and the packet must not promise an outcome. The court weighs the applicant's interests against the legitimate needs of the government under division (E)(3), must consider the prosecutor's stated reasons where an objection is filed, and must direct a probation officer to make inquiries and written reports. Division (F) directs the court to order expungement only once it has made the eligibility finding and found that the applicant's interests are not substantially outweighed by legitimate governmental needs.
determination.8_packetCapability: Packet-capable as a participant filing. There is a participant application, the statute prescribes its three required contents in division (C)(1) to (3), and the participant files it themselves in a court. Nothing about the mechanism prevents generation.
determination.9_isCustomPleadingStillTheCorrectStrateg: Yes, unchanged. No statewide official form exists for a section that took effect on 2026-03-20, the statute prescribes the application's contents, and a generated document therefore has a specification to be audited against. The memo's recorded outputStrategy of custom_pleading is correct and this record supplies no reason to change it.
determination.10_isASeparateRouteOrNodeRequired: No. There is no second mechanism to model, so there is no track, component, supporting action or composed unit to add. The single primary_filing component the memo carries is the correct shape.
determination.11_doesTheExistingCleanTrackSplitRemainV: Yes. oh_2953_33_nonconviction, oh_2953_32_sealing, oh_2953_32_expungement and oh_2953_35_firearm are unaffected, and so are the three process-guidance routes and the deferred oh_automatic_sealing node. Nothing in this record moves any of them, and the marijuana route's separation from them is confirmed rather than disturbed: section 2953.321 is its own section with its own eligibility set, its own fee and its own hearing timetable.
determination.12_theReleaseBlockerCanBeClosed: Yes, on this question. The governing-mechanism release blocker on oh_marijuana_expungement is answered and can be retired by whoever owns OH.memo.json. The track's other release blocker, about a local application form, is untouched and remains open.

memoAccuracyFindings.note: Two statements in the integrated memo do not match the enacted section. Neither is within this job's owned path and neither is corrected here; both are handed off, because a memo amendment is the right instrument and this record is not.

items.memoSays: The fee provision is cited as Ohio Rev. Code section 2953.321(H).
items.theSectionSays: The fee is at division (G). The section as enacted runs (A) to (G) and has no division (H).
items.severity: citation defect, participant-facing only through the fee statement

items.memoSays: "the prosecutor is notified at least 60 days before the hearing and may object at least 30 days before it".
items.theSectionSays: Division (D)(1) requires the court to notify the prosecutor of the hearing and permits the prosecutor to object "by filing an objection with the court prior to the date set for the hearing". It sets no 60-day notice period and no 30-day objection deadline. Those figures belong to the general conviction-sealing section, 2953.32, and do not govern this route. The Legislative Service Commission's Final Analysis describes the same rule the section does and supplies no such figures either.
items.severity: substantive. It is a participant-facing timetable that would be stated to a participant as law and is not law on this route.

residualQuestions.question: Whether Ohio courts have published a dedicated local application form for section 2953.321, and how many distinct local packets exist, for a section that took effect on 2026-03-20.
residualQuestions.whyNotABuildBlocker: The statute prescribes the application's contents, so the document can be drafted without knowing whether a given court also publishes a form. What the local-form position changes is the filing instruction, not the pleading.

residualQuestions.question: How a participant establishes indigency for the purposes of the division (G) fee waiver, and whether any court requires a particular affidavit or form for it. The section says only "unless indigent" and prescribes no procedure.

Division (D)(1) requires the court to direct a probation officer to make inquiries and written reports concerning the applicant. What that involves in practice, how long it takes, and whether the applicant is interviewed, is not established by the section and is not established here.
residualQuestions.whyItMatters: It is participant-facing expectation-setting on a route where a hearing is mandatory and an investigation precedes it. A packet that does not mention it understates what the participant is signing up for.

residualQuestions.question: Section 2953.321 reaches only dispositions occurring before 2026-03-20 and is drafted as a one-off remedial window rather than an ongoing route. Whether the General Assembly later extends it, or adds an automatic mechanism, is a monitoring question.
residualQuestions.whyRecorded: The population this track serves is closed and will only shrink. That is a product fact worth knowing, and a later amendment would be a material change.

residualQuestions.question: The Legislative Service Commission's Final Analysis was retrieved over a connection whose certificate chain could not be verified.
residualQuestions.analysis: Low consequence. Every operative fact taken from it was independently confirmed against the codified text over a valid connection, and the determination does not depend on it.

residualQuestions.question: Whether Ohio's separate sealing regime for records already covered by other chapter 2953 routes should ever be offered to the same participant alongside this one is a product-scope question, not a legal one.

blockerClassification.buildBlockersRemaining: None on this question. The governing mechanism is established.
blockerClassification.releaseBlockersRemaining: The local application form, the indigency procedure and the probation-report expectation. All three are participant-facing copy and filing instructions.
blockerClassification.monitoringQuestions: The pre-2026-03-20 cutoff and any later amendment; the transport caveat on the Final Analysis.
blockerClassification.productScopeBoundaries: Whether to offer overlapping chapter 2953 routes to one participant.

The two memo accuracy findings above should go to the same amendment: the fee division is (G) and not (H), and the 60-day notice and 30-day objection figures do not govern this route and should be replaced with what division (D) actually says.
The authoritative blocker ledger carries the governing-mechanism question as open on this track and can be closed against this record by its owner.

terminalDispositionDetail.why: The narrowest accurate result. It is not unresolved: three complete statutory enumerations and a Final Analysis all point the same way and the initiated statute's own chapter was read in full before it was repealed. It is not a finding that relief was created and taken away: nothing was there. And it is not a readiness statement: the track keeps its other release blocker and no packet becomes generatable.
terminalDispositionDetail.howTheNegativeWasEstablished: By enumeration, not by absence of a search result. Thirty-six sections of the initiated statute's chapter, thirty-nine of its successor, and forty-three of chapter 2953 were each listed and read for a record-clearing provision. One exists, and Senate Bill 56 created it.
